736.title: the lac house
736.hook: the brothers know the house will burn, and decide to stay in it, while a digger works beneath the floor
736.howItsDone: In tellings of the Mahabharata, the brothers' patience at Varanavata is told as the fruit of Yudhishthira's calm judgment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vidura's riddle, and Yudhishthira catching the smell of fat and lac. This house is made to burn.

Bhima's answer is the obvious one. If this house is made to burn, let's get out of it, back to where we were safe. It's the answer that comes first, standing in a room that smells of fuel. The walls look solid. The rooms are fine. Purochana is all smiles. And somewhere in the plaster is enough to turn the whole place into a torch. Yudhishthira says no. We stay.
screen: `BHIMA: LET'S GET OUT.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA: WE STAY.` → `A TEST OF NERVE.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira lays out his reasons. If we run, Purochana will know we've guessed, and he'll set the fire at once, or Duryodhana's people will hunt us down. We have no allies out here, no treasury, no army. So we'll live here as if we suspect nothing. We'll go hunting in the forests and learn every road and path, and we'll make a way out that nobody can see. Then help arrives: a skilled digger, sent by Vidura. He proves who he is by repeating words only Yudhishthira heard on the road, the riddle. Under the house, from the middle of it, he digs a passage leading out, and covers the opening level with the floor. All the while, Purochana keeps watch at the door, sure his guests know nothing. Look where the brothers' safety comes from. Not a battle, or a god, or a miracle: patience, attention, and an uncle who sent a quiet helper. Remember the riddle: a fire that burns a whole forest can't reach the creatures in holes underground. Now the brothers are making their hole. They eat in the house, sleep in the house, smile at Purochana, and wait, the text says, a long time, with weapons close at hand. A house built to look kind is answered by guests who look calm.

737.title: the lac house
737.hook: a feast, a family of strangers asleep, and a fire lit from the inside
737.carry: a woman and five sons, unnamed
737.howItsDone: Some Hindus read the Mahabharata straight through over months, a section at a time, as this serial does; others meet episodes like the lac house through storytelling, theater and television.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house: Yudhishthira chose to stay, calm on the surface, while Vidura's digger cut a passage under the floor.

The house at Varanavata was made to look like a gift and burn like a torch, with lac, resin and ghee worked into its walls, the text says. Under its floor is a different secret: a tunnel, dug by a miner Vidura sent, its mouth hidden inside the house. Kunti and her sons are living on top of a fire that hasn't been lit. Purochana, who built it, lives there too, waiting for his moment. Tonight, someone else strikes first.
screen: `A HOUSE MADE TO BURN.` → `A TUNNEL UNDER THE FLOOR.` → `TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kunti gives a feast. Brahmins come and eat, and women come, and when it's over the guests go home. But a Nishada woman, of the forest people, has come looking for food with her five sons. They eat and drink, and fall asleep in the house so heavily, the text says, they're like the dead. In the dark, Bhima gets up. He sets fire first to where Purochana sleeps, then to the door, then all around the house. The family goes down into the tunnel, and out. In the morning the townspeople stand at the ashes, grieving. They find Purochana, burned in his own trap. And they find a woman and five young men, and they say: Kunti and her sons are dead. Now stay with one detail. The plan works because strangers were in the house, and the text tells it quickly, without stopping for them. Some readers take it plainly: fate put those bodies there, and the world needed to believe. Some say the poem is showing the cost of the cousins' quarrel, beginning with people who had no part in it. Some notice that the woman and her sons are never named, and that the silence is itself worth hearing. The poem doesn't rule on the act. It shows it, and leaves room. The lac house was built to kill the Pandavas. It killed the man who built it, and six people nobody planned for.

738.title: the lac house
738.hook: Bhima carries his whole family through the dark, and a stranger at the river says the right words
738.carry: quiet help, hidden in plain sight
738.howItsDone: Vidura's counsel is read in its own right in Hindu tradition: the Vidura Niti, his advice to Dhritarashtra in the Udyoga Parva, is read by some as a book of practical wisdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house burned, and strangers' bodies were taken for the Pandavas'. Your line was a woman and five sons, unnamed.

Out of the tunnel, into a forest at night, with a town about to wake behind them. Kunti and her sons are worn out, and the dark is thick. So Bhima picks them all up. The text sets it out: his mother on his shoulders, the twins against his sides, Yudhishthira and Arjuna held by the hand. He pushes through the trees, carrying his whole family at once. The house is behind them. They still have to get away.
screen: `OUT OF THE TUNNEL.` → `BHIMA CARRIES THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: They reach the Ganga, and a man is waiting with a boat. He says Vidura sent him. But anyone could say that. So he gives the same kind of sign the digger gave: he speaks back words from Vidura's riddle on the road, words only Yudhishthira understood. Only someone Vidura trusted could know them. Yudhishthira hears them, and the family gets in. Look at what Vidura has done, start to finish. He couldn't stop the plot in the open. So he warned in a riddle, sent a miner to dig, and set a boat at the water's edge. None of it loud. Every piece hidden in plain sight. The boatman carries them across, sends them on with good wishes, and goes back the way he came. What runs through this part is trust. Bhima is trusted to carry everyone. The boatman is trusted on a few remembered words. And the whole family trusts Vidura, who isn't even there. A shared secret becomes a kind of key. Some readers see Vidura as the quiet conscience of the Kuru house: the one who can't change the king's mind, but keeps a door open anyway. And the Pandavas, dead as far as the world knows, step off on the far bank as people no one is looking for.

739.title: the lac house
739.hook: the city mourns the living, and in the forest Bhima keeps watch
739.howItsDone: Offering water for the dead, called tarpana, is part of Hindu funeral and remembrance rites; in this story the offering is made for the Pandavas while they are still alive.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nauka, the boat at the Ganga, its boatman proved by Vidura's own words. Your line was quiet help, hidden in plain sight.

In Hastinapura, the news arrives: the Pandavas are dead, burned at Varanavata with their mother. Dhritarashtra weeps, the text says, and orders the rites for the dead. Water is offered for them. The people mourn. Vidura grieves only a little, because he knows. Far away, the five brothers and their mother are alive, asleep on the ground. Two places, and two kinds of grief.

In the forest they've gone as far as they can. Kunti is exhausted and thirsty. Bhima goes for water, and by the time he's back they're all asleep on the bare ground under a tree. So Bhima sits up alone and looks at them. The text gives him a lament here. In paraphrase: what could hurt more than this, my brothers sleeping on the earth, my mother lying in the open. He thinks of Duryodhana, and his anger rises. He could go back and end it, he says. But Yudhishthira isn't angry, and Bhima won't move without him. So he stays, and keeps watch. Set the two scenes side by side. In the city, a king weeps for nephews his own son tried to kill, and the text doesn't tell us how to weigh those tears. Vidura holds his secret and says little. In the forest, the brother known for his strength, and for his anger, spends it sitting still. Bhima is the brother we first met shaking boys out of a tree. Here, at the end of the lac house, his strength takes another shape: he stays awake so the others can rest. The house is ash. The family is homeless, mourned as dead, sleeping in the open. And one of them watches over the rest.

740.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
740.hook: a daughter rises from a sacrificial fire, and a king announces she will choose
740.carry: a princess born from the fire
740.howItsDone: Draupadi is honored as a goddess in parts of South India: some villages in Tamil Nadu keep temples to Draupadi Amman and hold festivals in her name, some with firewalking.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bhima under the tree, awake while his family slept. Your line was strength that keeps watch.

A king has a fire lit because he wants a son. Drupada of Panchala has been humbled by Drona, and he wants someone who can answer that. Priests perform a great sacrifice. From the fire a young man rises, armed and shining: Dhrishtadyumna. Then, from the middle of the altar, a young woman. Dark, the text says, with eyes like lotus petals, and the scent of blue lotus around her. The sacrifice was for a son. The fire gives a daughter too.
screen: `A FIRE FOR A SON.` → `A DAUGHTER FROM THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: As she rises, the text says, a voice is heard from the sky: this dark girl will bring about the destruction of the warrior class. She's named Krishnaa, the dark one, and also Draupadi, Drupada's daughter, and Panchali, the princess of Panchala. The Pandavas, still hiding as brahmins in a town, hear it all from a traveling brahmin: the fire, the brother and sister, and the swayamvara Drupada has announced. A swayamvara is a choosing: a princess's own choosing of a husband, with the suitors gathered in one place. In another story the Mahabharata tells, Nala and Damayanti's, the princess walks among her suitors and garlands the one she wants. Drupada's will work differently, and tomorrow we'll see how. For now, look at who's standing in the doorway of the story. A woman born from a fire, with a prophecy spoken over her before she's said a word. A father with an old wound. And five brothers the world thinks are dead, listening to a traveler's news in a borrowed room. Kunti sees her sons grow restless at the news, the text says, and says it's time to move on, to Panchala. So they set out, still dressed as brahmins.
screen: `A VOICE FROM THE SKY.` · `KRISHNAA, DRAUPADI, PANCHALI.` · `A SWAYAMVARA: HER CHOOSING.` · `THE PANDAVAS SET OUT.`

741.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
741.hook: a bow almost no one can bend, and a mark beyond a device set high in the air
741.carry: the kings fall, one by one
741.howItsDone: The contest at Panchala, with the bow and the mark, is shown in Hindu painting, dance and storytelling; in some retellings the archer aims at a fish's eye seen reflected in water below.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara was announced: a princess born from the fire, and five brothers setting out for Panchala.

The arena at Panchala is packed. Kings and princes have come from far and wide, dressed in their best. Brahmins have come to watch. There's music, and the noise of a crowd that has waited for this. Somewhere among the brahmins sit five brothers in borrowed clothes, whom everyone here believes are dead. Then Draupadi enters, carrying a garland, and her brother Dhrishtadyumna rises to announce the terms.
screen: `A PACKED ARENA.` → `FIVE BROTHERS IN DISGUISE.` → `THE TERMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the challenge, in paraphrase. This is the bow, these are the arrows. Up high is a mark, and in front of it a device set in the air, with an opening in it. Whoever strings the bow, shoots through the opening and hits the mark, and is worthy in birth and form and strength, wins my sister. Now a detail the text gives. Drupada had hoped all along to give his daughter to Arjuna, so he had this bow made so stiff that hardly anyone could string it. One by one, the kings try, and the bow beats them. Some can't bend it at all. Some get close, and it springs back and throws them to the ground, their crowns and ornaments scattered across the floor. Great names, humbled in front of everyone. Here's what makes this swayamvara strange. The word means the bride's own choosing. But her choice runs through a test her father set, shaped around one man he hoped would come. The text doesn't say what Draupadi made of it. It shows her standing with the garland while her brother reads out the terms, and the kings walk up to the bow. Some retellings picture the mark as a fish's eye, seen in a reflection. In this passage it's simply a mark, beyond a device, very high up.
screen: `THE TERMS: STRING, SHOOT, HIT.` · `A BOW MADE FOR ONE MAN.` · `THE KINGS FALL, ONE BY ONE.` · `A CHOOSING, ROUTED THROUGH A TEST.`

742.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
742.hook: Karna strings the bow, and one sentence stops him
742.howItsDone: Karna's story is retold in Hindu storytelling, theater and dance, and in modern novels, some of which tell the whole Mahabharata from his side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stiff bow, the mark set high, and kings thrown to the floor. Your line was the kings fall, one by one.

As the kings give up, one by one, a man rises whom we've met before. Karna. Found in a basket on the river, raised by a charioteer, born with armor on his body. The bow has just thrown kings to the floor in front of everyone. Karna walks up to it.
screen: `THE KINGS GIVE UP.` → `KARNA RISES.` → `HE WALKS TO THE BOW.`

segments.voice: In the version Ganguli translated, Karna lifts the bow and strings it. He fits the arrows. He's about to shoot. And Draupadi speaks, loudly, so the whole arena hears. In paraphrase: I will not choose a suta for my husband. A suta: a charioteer, a charioteer's son. Karna laughs, a bitter laugh, the text says. He glances up at the sun, and puts the bow down. A few lines, and they land on everything we've heard about Karna these past weeks: the basket on the river, Adhiratha the charioteer and his wife Radha, who raised him, the name Radheya. Birth deciding who may compete. Readers hear this moment in different ways. Some hear Draupadi holding the contest to its own terms: her brother announced that birth would count. Some hear her guarding her father's hope for Arjuna. Some hear the old sting of birth used against a man who could clearly do the thing. And some hear all of these at once. The poem doesn't settle it; it moves on. But stay with that glance at the sun. The sun, as we know and the arena doesn't, is Karna's father. He looks up to him in the moment he's turned away, without knowing who he's looking at. Karna and Draupadi will meet again in another hall, later in this serial. This week began in the lac house. It ends with a bow back on the ground, and the arena waiting for someone else.
screen: `KARNA STRINGS THE BOW.` · `I WILL NOT CHOOSE A SUTA.` · `A LAUGH, AND A GLANCE AT THE SUN.` · `MANY WAYS TO HEAR ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: When the bow went down, Karna looked up at the sun, not knowing whose face he was looking for. Bring to mind where you turn when something closes on you: a person, a place, a prayer, a habit, a patch of sky. Don't judge it; just notice whether it holds you, and rest there a few breaths.
